title: An asymmetric atom-photon architecture for device-independent quantum key distribution over 25\,km
authors: Jonas Meiers, Christian Haen, Max Bergerhoff, Pascal Baumgart, Tobias Bauer, Christoph Becher, Jürgen Eschner
abstract: Device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD) can guarantee security without trusting the internal workings of the measurement devices, but extending it to fiber networks demands high-quality entanglement, reliable heralding, and faithful photon transmission simultaneously. Here, we address these requirements in an event-ready asymmetric atom-photon architecture implemented over $25\,\mathrm{km}$ of spooled telecom fiber. A single trapped $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ ion forms one party of the protocol while a single transmitted photon measured at the remote station forms the other. Double quantum frequency conversion and active polarization stabilization preserve the atom-photon quantum correlation across the full link. We obtain a Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt parameter of $|S|=2.75^{+0.16}_{-0.15}$, exceeding the threshold $|S|=2.362$ required for a positive asymptotic secret-key fraction under the DIQKD model used. Within the same asymptotic model, this corresponds to a conservative estimate of 69 secret-key bits out of 10908 detected Bell states. The demonstrated architecture establishes a route towards DIQKD in heterogeneous, repeater-compatible quantum networks.
summary: The paper presents an experimental realization of Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD) over 25 km using an asymmetric architecture combining a trapped $^{40}	ext{Ca}^+$ ion and a transmitted photon. By maintaining quantum correlations across the fiber link using frequency conversion and polarization stabilization, the team demonstrated a high CHSH parameter, proving a viable route for quantum networking.
main_problem: The primary goal is to demonstrate Device-Independent Quantum Key Distribution (DIQKD) over a practical, long-distance fiber network of 25 km.
main_result: The authors successfully achieved a CHSH parameter $|S|=2.75$, exceeding the required threshold, and estimated a secure key rate of 69 bits out of 10908 detected states.
method: The protocol uses an event-ready, asymmetric atom-photon architecture where a trapped $^{40}	ext{Ca}^+$ ion acts as one party and a transmitted photon acts as the other.
model_or_system: The system couples a single trapped $^{40}	ext{Ca}^+$ ion to a photon transmitted over 25 km of telecom fiber. Key components include double quantum frequency conversion, active polarization stabilization, and SNSPD detection.
key_observables: Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt parameter ($|S|$), secret-key bits (SKB), and readout-failure probability ($	ext{p}_{	ext{fail}}$).
important_parameters: Link distance of 25 km; DIQKD threshold $|S|=2.362$; Signal-to-Background Ratio (SBR) $\approx 10$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the protocol is event-ready and that the architecture is compatible with heterogeneous, repeater-compatible quantum networks.
figures_summary: Figure 1 provides a schematic of the entire atom-photon QKD link, while Figure 2 details the relevant energy levels and transitions of the $^{40}	ext{Ca}^+$ ion used for entanglement generation.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup, including the complex optical and atomic control sequences (QFC, APC, laser cooling/readout), followed by the measurement statistics analysis (testing for setting dependence) and finally the calculation of the security parameters ($|S|$ and SKB).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenges of scaling quantum communication, specifically by integrating trapped-ion quantum memories with long-haul fiber links in a device-independent framework.

figures.caption: FIG. 2. Scheme showing relevant 40Ca+ levels and transitions used for atom-photon entanglement generation and atomic state readout. Excitation from S1/2 to P3/2 (blue arrow) pre- pares the excited state, subsequent spontaneous decay to D5/2 generates a single photon (wavy red arrows) whose polariza- tion is entangled with the Zeeman sublevel in D5/2. Sub- sequent laser pulses (purple arrows) coherently transfer the atomic qubit state from D5/2 to S1/2, where an RF pulse with variable phase rotates the measurement basis. Final state readout employs shelving pulses and state-selective fluores- cence (see text).

FIG. 1. Schematic of the atom-photon QKD link. A trapped 40Ca+ ion emits 854 nm photons that are frequency-converted to the telecom C-band (1550 nm), transmitted over 25 km of fiber, converted back to 854 nm, and analyzed in polarization using single-photon detectors (SNSPDs). A separate classical fiber distributes White Rabbit timing and transmits electronic heralding signals from Bob to Alice to trigger the ion readout. Active polarization stabilization (APC) is applied on the quantum fiber to compensate slow drifts. For more details, see text.
